title: Scintillation of the first-known pulsar planetary system
summary: We present a scintillation study of the first-known pulsar planetary system, PSR~B1257+12, using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). A total of 31 observations with durations greater than or equal to 30 minutes were analyzed. For 14 longer observations (greater than or equal to 120 minutes), one-dimensional autocorrelation function analyses yielded the scintillation timescale, scintillation bandwidth, and frequency-drift rate for 12 epochs. Two observations show strong periodic modulation in the frequency-domain auto-correlation function, likely caused by astronomical-unit-scale structures along the propagation path, preventing reliable measurements of the scintillation timescale and bandwidth. In three observations, secondary spectra reveal simultaneous detections of inner, middle, and outer arcs. Analysis of the annual modulation of the inner-arc curvature indicates isotropic scattering, with a screen distance of $233\pm28$~pc and transverse velocity $V_{\rm scr,α}=-7.16\pm2.16$ km~s$^{-1}$, $V_{\rm scr,δ}=-41.07\pm5.69$ km~s$^{-1}$. Delay-profile analysis for both the inner and outer arcs suggest spectral exponents consistent with, or smaller than, the Kolmogorov value. Under isotropic scattering, the screen--pulsar distances are $354\pm22$~pc and $166\pm12$~pc for the middle and outer arcs. Combining the results from long-term timing analyses with our scintillation measurements, we find that the dispersion measure (DM) variations are primarily dominated by plasma located further away from the pulsar. The low DM-change rate of the outer arc and the absence of nearby scattering screens suggest that the immediate environment of the pulsar may be relatively clean. Alternatively, scattering screens closer to the pulsar may exist but remain undetected, requiring higher-sensitivity or longer-duration observations.

AI.tldr: Using FAST observations, scintillation analysis of PSR B1257+12 shows isotropic scattering from distant screens dominating plasma effects; nearby environment seems clean but undetected local scattering screens cannot be ruled out.
AI.motivation: To investigate the scintillation properties of the first-known pulsar planetary system PSR B1257+12 to understand the scattering environment and plasma distribution along the line of sight.
AI.method: Analyzed 31 FAST observations (≥30 min each), using one-dimensional autocorrelation function analysis on 14 long observations (≥120 min) to measure scintillation parameters, and secondary spectral analysis to probe scattering arcs and their properties.
AI.result: Detected isotropic scattering with measured screen distance around 233 pc and transverse velocities; identified multiple scattering arcs with distances estimated for middle and outer arcs; found DM variations dominated by plasma far from the pulsar, suggesting a relatively clean local environment or undetected nearby screens.
AI.conclusion: Scintillation studies reveal that the bulk of dispersion measure variations arise from distant plasma rather than near the pulsar; the pulsar's immediate vicinity appears relatively free of scattering screens unless undetected by current observations; further sensitive, long-duration measurements are required to detect possible nearby scattering structures.

title: Evidence for protostellar jets as a population of hadronic gamma-ray sources
summary: Stars are born in darkness, deep within cold, dense molecular clouds where gravity drives the collapse of gas and dust, giving rise to protostars, the earliest stages of stellar evolution. Once considered purely thermal sources, these young systems are now emerging as sites of energetic non-thermal activity. While radio synchrotron jets hinted at the presence of relativistic electrons, direct confirmation of proton acceleration remained elusive. Here we report a statistically significant detection of gamma rays from a population of young stellar objects, revealing a Galactic class of Gamma-Loud Protostars. Observations point towards particle acceleration within protostellar jets, where gamma-ray emission arises from protons interacting with surrounding molecular clouds via pion decay. We find a correlation between cosmic-ray output and bolometric luminosity, suggesting that particle acceleration scales with the system's mechanical power. These findings open a new observational window into the role of non-thermal processes in protostellar evolution and suggest that gamma-ray studies of protostars can provide critical insights into accretion, ejection, and feedback in star formation. This previously overlooked emission traces the energetic feedback that young stars inject into their surroundings, shaping the conditions for subsequent star and planet formation.

AI.tldr: Gamma-ray emission from young protostars confirms proton acceleration in their jets, uncovering an energetic feedback mechanism that shapes star and planet formation.
AI.motivation: To investigate the presence and role of non-thermal energetic activity, specifically proton acceleration, in young stellar objects (protostars) and their impact on star formation.
AI.method: Detection and analysis of gamma rays emitted by a population of young stellar objects, focusing on the interaction of protons within protostellar jets and surrounding molecular clouds, supported by correlations between cosmic-ray output and bolometric luminosity.
AI.result: Statistically significant detection of gamma rays from Gamma-Loud Protostars, confirming proton acceleration within protostellar jets; established that particle acceleration is correlated with system mechanical power and influences stellar environment feedback.
AI.conclusion: Protostellar jets accelerate protons leading to gamma-ray emission via pion decay, revealing a previously overlooked energetic feedback mechanism in young stars that affects accretion, ejection, and star and planet formation processes.

title: Damping of Fast Radio Bursts in the Inner Magnetospheres of Magnetars
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, submitted to the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: We investigate the propagation of fast radio bursts (FRBs) through magnetar magnetospheres. Previous work showed that, in the inner magnetosphere, GHz radio waves propagate as fast magnetosonic waves and undergo resonant three-wave interactions that transfer their energy into trapped Alfvén waves. Using three-dimensional force-free electrodynamics simulations, we demonstrate that FRBs would excite Alfvénic fluctuations, leading to strong nonlinear attenuation of the radio signal. In quiescent dipolar magnetospheres, the nonlinear decay stays efficient within $\sim10$--$100$ magnetar radii; charge starvation of the excited Alfvén waves stops the decay at larger radii. For FRBs propagating within relativistic magnetic outflows launched during magnetospheric eruptions, three-wave interactions remain efficient and constrain the escape radius to $\gtrsim10^2$--$10^3$ magnetar radii for luminous bursts. Our results confirm that nonlinear plasma processes strongly limit the escape of FRBs from the inner magnetospheres of magnetars.

AI.tldr: FRBs traveling through magnetar magnetospheres undergo nonlinear interactions that significantly attenuate their radio signals, restricting their escape primarily beyond several hundred magnetar radii, as shown by 3D force-free electrodynamics simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand how fast radio bursts (FRBs) propagate through magnetar magnetospheres and the impact of plasma interactions on their escape.
AI.method: Three-dimensional force-free electrodynamics simulations were used to study the nonlinear interactions between GHz radio waves and Alfvén waves in magnetar magnetospheres.
AI.result: FRBs excite Alfvénic fluctuations causing strong nonlinear attenuation of the radio signal within 10 to 100 magnetar radii in quiescent dipolar magnetospheres, with decay limited by charge starvation at larger radii. In relativistic magnetic outflows from magnetospheric eruptions, three-wave interactions remain efficient, limiting FRB escape to beyond 100 to 1000 magnetar radii for luminous bursts.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear plasma processes, particularly resonant three-wave interactions transferring energy from fast magnetosonic waves to Alfvén waves, strongly limit the ability of FRBs to escape from the inner magnetospheres of magnetars.

title: Nonlinear Decay of Fast Magnetosonic Waves through Weak Turbulence: Force-Free Electrodynamics Simulations
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We investigate the propagation of low-frequency fast-magnetosonic (FMS) waves in highly magnetized environments. Such conditions are relevant to the escape of GHz fast radio bursts potentially produced in the inner magnetospheres of magnetars. It remains an open question whether such waves can escape without substantial reprocessing. Using relativistic force-free electrodynamics simulations, we confirm the key theoretical predictions of Golbraikh & Lyubarsky (2023) and demonstrate that FMS waves undergo efficient nonlinear conversion into secondary FMS and Alfvén waves via the parametric decay instability. This process continues to drain energy from the primary FMS waves even after approximate energy equipartition between the FMS and Alfvén components is established. The resulting spectrum of excited waves is broad, extending across much of the inertial range in $k$-space within the simulation domain. Our results indicate that FMS waves likely do not escape magnetar magnetospheres without substantial dissipation and spectral broadening.

AI.tldr: Simulations show that low-frequency fast-magnetosonic waves in magnetar magnetospheres are strongly damped through nonlinear parametric decay into secondary waves, preventing their direct escape and implying substantial energy dissipation and spectral broadening before emission as fast radio bursts.
AI.motivation: To understand the propagation and escape mechanisms of low-frequency fast-magnetosonic waves in highly magnetized environments relevant to fast radio bursts from magnetars.
AI.method: Relativistic force-free electrodynamics simulations were employed to test theoretical predictions regarding the nonlinear evolution and conversion of FMS waves in magnetar magnetospheres.
AI.result: FMS waves undergo efficient nonlinear parametric decay into secondary FMS and Alfvén waves, resulting in energy drainage from the primary waves, a broad wave spectrum, and significant dissipation and spectral broadening, suggesting that these waves do not escape magnetar magnetospheres without substantial reprocessing.
AI.conclusion: Low-frequency FMS waves generated in magnetar magnetospheres are likely unable to escape freely due to efficient nonlinear interactions causing energy loss and spectral broadening, challenging scenarios where GHz fast radio bursts directly emerge from inner magnetospheres without significant modification.

title: Physics-guided discovery of dynamical dark-energy equations of state through iterative AI reasoning
summary: Phenomenological model building has traditionally relied on human reasoning: equations are proposed from theoretical intuition, analogy, or empirical convenience, and only then tested against data. Here we show that this cycle can be recast as an iterative AI reasoning process for dynamical dark energy. Our framework uses a large language model to propose equations of state together with cosmological rationales, grounded by retrieval from the dark-energy literature and refined through autonomous evaluation. Each candidate is embedded in a cosmological model, optimized against observations, and assessed using likelihood performance and theoretical consistency. An independent language-model critic scores the physical motivation, novelty, clarity, stability and implementation validity of both the equation and its rationale, allowing subsequent proposals to evolve jointly in mathematical structure and physical reasoning. Applied to cosmological data combinations including supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations and Planck likelihoods, the framework identifies two parameterizations that, to the best of our knowledge, have not previously been explored and that are competitive with established forms. For Pantheon+ supernovae, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations and the full Planck 2018 temperature, polarization, and lensing likelihoods, the best AI-selected model attains larger Bayesian evidence than the traditional parameterizations considered here by more than one unit. These results show that AI-guided reasoning can complement physical model building by proposing and evaluating interpretable phenomenological parameterizations for dynamical dark energy.

AI.tldr: An AI-driven iterative framework proposes and assesses new equations for dynamical dark energy, discovering novel parameterizations that outperform established models using cosmological data, demonstrating AI's potential to advance phenomenological model building.
AI.motivation: Traditional phenomenological model building depends heavily on human intuition and empirical methods to propose theoretical equations, which can limit exploration and discovery.
AI.method: The authors develop an AI framework that integrates a large language model to iteratively propose, rationalize, and refine equations of state for dynamical dark energy, embedding candidates in cosmological models, optimizing against observational data, and using an independent language-model critic to evaluate physical and theoretical validity.
AI.result: The framework discovered two novel parameterizations for dynamical dark energy that outperform traditional models in Bayesian evidence when applied to comprehensive cosmological datasets including supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and Planck data.
AI.conclusion: AI-guided reasoning effectively complements traditional model building by autonomously generating interpretable and competitive phenomenological models for dynamical dark energy, enhancing the discovery process beyond human-driven methods.

title: Short-Range Forces Can Catalyze Extreme Orbital Evolution in Hierarchical Triples
summary: Hierarchical triples are promising environments for producing exotica such as black hole mergers and hot Jupiters, because of the von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai (ZLK) effect, whereby a distant tertiary can torque an inner binary to high eccentricity over secular timescales. In the double-averaged (DA) approximation to ZLK, this eccentricity excitation is suppressed by apsidal precession due to `short-range forces' (SRFs) like relativity and tidal/rotational bulges. Here we show that, when the DA approximation is relaxed, SRFs often catalyze, rather than suppress, extreme eccentricity behavior. This occurs because SRFs can drive large, discrete jumps in the binary's effective `adiabatic invariants' during high-eccentricity episodes. These nonadiabatic jumps can dramatically alter the maximum/minimum eccentricity and secular period of astrophysically relevant triples, including some for which SRFs were previously thought irrelevant. Even the angular momentum component $j_z$ evolves secularly -- to our knowledge, this is the first time such evolution has been demonstrated from a quadrupole-order, three-body mechanism. In short, binaries may explore much more of phase space than is implied by any (semi-)analytic ZLK theory of which we are aware. We demonstrate this at the test-particle quadrupole level; in a companion paper we show how even more-extreme behavior occurs when the jumps are combined with octupolar ZLK evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that in hierarchical triple systems, short-range forces can trigger extreme eccentricity changes by causing sudden jumps in orbital invariants when the double-averaged approximation is lifted, revealing more complex and extensive dynamical behavior than previously understood.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical triple systems offer environments for exotic astrophysical phenomena through the von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai effect, but existing double-averaged approximations fail to capture the full impact of short-range forces on eccentricity excitation.
AI.method: The study relaxes the double-averaged approximation in modeling the ZLK effect and investigates the role of short-range forces in driving nonadiabatic jumps in adiabatic invariants during high-eccentricity episodes, focusing on the test-particle quadrupole level analysis.
AI.result: Short-range forces, previously thought to suppress eccentricity growth, actually catalyze extreme eccentricity behavior by causing discrete jumps in adiabatic invariants, altering eccentricity extrema and secular periods. The study also reveals secular evolution in the angular momentum component $j_z$ via a quadrupole-order three-body mechanism, indicating greater phase space exploration than prior ZLK theories suggest.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing the double-averaged approximation unveils that short-range forces can enhance rather than dampen eccentricity excitations in hierarchical triples, fundamentally changing the dynamical understanding of these systems and expanding the known behavior beyond classical ZLK theory.

title: Cooling, conduction, compact objects: Gravothermal evolution of dissipative self-interacting dark matter halos
comment: 19 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables; to be submitted to A&A
summary: Many proposed self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models give rise to radiative processes that can dissipate energy. Understanding their impact on astrophysical objects through simulations and comparing the results with observations may thus constrain SIDM models. In this work, we systematically investigate how dissipation alters the gravothermal evolution of isolated SIDM halos by independently varying dissipation and heat conduction and identify potential observational signatures. To this end, we present the first extension of the $N$-body formalism for frequent small-angle self-interactions (fSIDM) to include effective dissipation. We compare all results for isolated halos with a dissipative gravothermal fluid model to assess its validity and limitations. We find that dissipation qualitatively changes the gravothermal evolution of SIDM halos beyond simply accelerating collapse. Sufficiently strong central cooling can invert the usual role of heat conduction: the formation of an isothermal core is suppressed such that conduction remains directed inward throughout the evolution. Outer halo regions beyond the scale radius can cool efficiently rather than being heated by conduction, resulting in a larger region of mass infall and a less pronounced indentation between the core and the outer halo in the final density profile. These effects depend strongly on the cooling rate but are comparatively insensitive to the angular dependence of the self-interaction cross section. We further show that weakly dissipative self-interactions can explain the properties of the recently observed strong lens perturber in JVAS~B1938+666 with significantly shorter evolution times or, equivalently, smaller cross sections compared to the elastic case. Our results open a new route to connecting halo structure and recently reported compact objects to dark-sector microphysics.

AI.tldr: This study extends N-body simulations of self-interacting dark matter to include dissipation, revealing that dissipation drastically changes halo evolution and structure, offering new observational signatures to constrain dark matter models and explaining lensing phenomena more efficiently than non-dissipative models.
AI.motivation: To understand how radiative dissipation processes in self-interacting dark matter models affect the gravothermal evolution of halos and to identify distinct observational signatures that could constrain such SIDM models through simulations.
AI.method: Extended the N-body formalism for frequent small-angle self-interactions to include effective dissipation; conducted systematic simulations varying dissipation and heat conduction; compared results with a dissipative gravothermal fluid model to validate and identify limitations.
AI.result: Dissipation changes halo evolution qualitatively by suppressing isothermal core formation, causing inward-directed conduction, cooling outer halo regions, and modifying density profiles. Weak dissipation models explain the properties of a strong lens perturber with shorter evolution times and smaller cross sections than elastic models, offering a new connection between halo structure and dark-sector physics.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation in self-interacting dark matter halos qualitatively alters their gravothermal evolution beyond accelerating collapse; strong central cooling suppresses core formation and inverts heat conduction direction, modifying halo density profiles. Weak dissipation explains certain astrophysical observations better than elastic models, linking halo structure to dark-sector microphysics.

title: On the Contribution of Local Sources to the Galactic Cosmic-Ray Spectrum: An Exact Series Solution for Two-Zone Diffusion
comment: submitted to PRD, The code accompanying this paper will be released soon
summary: Measurements of cosmic-ray proton and helium spectra below the knee show deviations from simple power laws, including multi-TeV structures. A possible explanation is that one or a few nearby sources contribute an additional component to the local spectrum. However, previous study shows that a dominant local contribution is statistically unlikely under a homogeneous diffusion model. In this work, we investigate how this probability changes if cosmic rays experience inefficient transport near their sources, motivated by observations of extended gamma-ray emission around Galactic accelerators. We derive a series Green's function that enables fast calculation of the particle distribution in this scenario, making Monte Carlo calculations for Galactic source populations feasible. The inner slow-diffusion region delays escape and redistributes the arriving particles in time and energy. In Monte Carlo realizations, the probability that the strongest local source becomes comparable to the background at $10\,\rm{TeV}$ increases from about $0.4\%$ in homogeneous diffusion to $1.7$--$2.2\%$ in the two-zone models. Thus inhibited near-source transport weakens, but does not remove, the statistical difficulty. We then examine cataloged nearby candidate supernova remnants and show that a $10\,\rm{TeV}$ feature can be reproduced only with additional assumptions, especially a harder local injection spectrum and a favorable diffusion coefficient. The predicted contribution of a given source changes strongly among different particle transport model. Therefore, the local source interpretations are plausible but highly model dependent, and require independent constraints on source injection history, particle transport mechanisms, and local interstellar turbulence.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how slow diffusion near cosmic-ray sources affects the likelihood of a local source dominating the 10 TeV cosmic-ray spectrum. Using a new Green's function approach and Monte Carlo simulations, it finds the probability increases but remains low, requiring specific injection and transport assumptions for local sources to explain observed spectral features.
AI.motivation: To explain deviations from simple power laws in cosmic-ray proton and helium spectra below the knee, particularly multi-TeV structures possibly contributed by nearby sources, and to assess the probability of a dominant local source contribution under different cosmic-ray transport models.
AI.method: Investigates cosmic-ray transport with inefficient diffusion near sources by deriving a series Green's function for fast particle distribution calculations, enabling Monte Carlo simulations of Galactic source populations; compares homogeneous diffusion and two-zone slow-diffusion models; examines cataloged nearby supernova remnants under varying transport assumptions.
AI.result: The probability that a local source dominates the cosmic-ray spectrum at 10 TeV increases from ~0.4% in homogeneous diffusion to 1.7–2.2% in two-zone slow-diffusion models, indicating inhibited near-source transport reduces but does not eliminate the statistical challenge. Reproducing observed spectral features requires additional assumptions like harder injection spectra and specific diffusion coefficients, making local source interpretations plausible but strongly model dependent.
AI.conclusion: Inhibited transport near sources moderately increases the likelihood of a local source significantly contributing to observed cosmic-ray spectra below the knee, but does not fully resolve statistical difficulties. Local source interpretations remain viable only with favorable assumptions on injection spectra and diffusion, highlighting the need for independent constraints on particle transport, source history, and interstellar turbulence.

title: BayeSN $\times$ Dovekie: Joint Photometric Cross-calibration and SED Modelling of Type Ia Supernovae
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present a new framework for BayeSN, the hierarchical Bayesian SED model for type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), incorporating cross-calibration of samples observed across heterogeneous telescopes. This framework is the first to parametrise the filter wavelength and zero-point offsets commonly used in SN~Ia cosmology within SN SED model training, enabling additional constraint on cross-calibration from SNe beyond the standard stellar-based cross-calibration pipeline. We apply this framework to train a new G26 BayeSN model on the same SED model training sample used in recent cosmological analyses, an order-of-magnitude increase over previous BayeSN training samples, and include a novel training methodology to leverage high-redshift SNe Ia in BayeSN training. We present the G26 model and apply it to the DES-SN5YR sample to assess performance, finding a 12 per cent reduction in $σ_{\rm NMAD}$ scatter when compared with SALT3.Dovekie; 0.164 mag compared with 0.185 mag for a sample of likely SNe Ia at $z < 0.7$, without bias corrections. We additionally present constraints on cross-calibration wavelength and zero-point shifts from our framework when using the latest `Dovekie' calibration constraints as a prior. This work is a key step towards a full end-to-end cosmological analysis with BayeSN; the new G26 model is incorporated within the public BayeSN code.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the G26 BayeSN hierarchical Bayesian SED model that integrates cross-calibration parameters to improve type Ia supernova cosmology. Trained on a significantly larger and higher-redshift inclusive sample, G26 reduces scatter by 12% compared to SALT3 and constrains calibration systematics, advancing towards comprehensive cosmological analyses with public BayeSN code.
AI.motivation: To improve the accuracy and robustness of type Ia supernova cosmology by addressing cross-calibration challenges arising from heterogeneous telescopes and increasing the training sample size, including high-redshift data, within the BayeSN SED modeling framework.
AI.method: The paper introduces a hierarchical Bayesian SED model framework, explicitly parameterizing filter wavelength and zero-point offsets to integrate cross-calibration in SN Ia SED model training. This framework is applied to train the G26 BayeSN model with an expanded training sample including high-redshift SNe Ia and uses updated calibration priors for robust cross-calibration constraint estimation.
AI.result: The G26 model trained with the new framework achieves a 12% reduction in normalized median absolute deviation (σ_NMAD) scatter (0.164 mag vs. 0.185 mag) compared to SALT3.Dovekie on a low-redshift sample (z<0.7), without bias corrections. It further provides quantitative constraints on cross-calibration wavelength and zero-point shifts when incorporating Dovekie calibration priors.
AI.conclusion: The newly developed G26 BayeSN model demonstrates improved photometric scatter reduction compared to previous models, indicating enhanced performance for type Ia supernova cosmology analyses. Incorporating cross-calibration parameters within the hierarchical Bayesian SED framework enables better calibration constraints leveraging supernova data beyond traditional stellar methods.

title: On the braking index evolution of PSR B0540-69: wind braking of pulsars
summary: The pulsar PSR B0450-69 has both a braking index measurement and spin-down state change. After its spin-down state change, it shows an increasing braking index with time. Previously, it is pointed out that the spin-down state change may be caused by an enhanced particle wind. The prediction is that its braking index in the high spin-down state will be smaller. The current measured braking index is approaching the previous prediction. The transient variation of braking index may be due to a small varying part of the particle number density. The final braking index evolution is found to be in an exponential form. The braking index of PSR B0540-69 is expected to approach some steady value. Future braking index measurement may make clear the physics for the braking index evolution. It may also help to make test different particle acceleration potential in the pulsar magnetosphere. Finally, a phenomenological treatment of wind braking model of pulsars is presented. It can simplify the applications to pulsar braking index, intermittent pulsars and PSR B0540-69.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the braking index evolution of pulsar PSR B0450-69 after a spin-down state change, showing it increases exponentially towards a steady value due to particle wind effects, and presents a simplified wind braking model applicable to similar pulsars.
AI.motivation: To understand the evolution of the braking index of pulsar PSR B0450-69 after its spin-down state change and to explore the underlying physical mechanisms related to particle wind effects.
AI.method: Analyzing observational braking index measurements for PSR B0450-69, interpreting the transient variations through a model involving particle number density changes, and applying a phenomenological wind braking model to explain pulsar braking index behavior.
AI.result: The braking index of PSR B0450-69 shows an increasing trend post spin-down state change, consistent with predictions of a smaller braking index during high spin-down states. The evolution follows an exponential form and is expected to reach a steady value, which can inform testing particle acceleration potentials in the pulsar magnetosphere. The wind braking model provides a simplified framework for interpreting braking indices in pulsars including PSR B0540-69 and intermittent pulsars.
AI.conclusion: The braking index evolution of PSR B0450-69 is governed by changes in particle wind, exhibiting an exponential trend towards a steady state. This supports the wind braking model as a useful tool to understand pulsar spin-down behavior and particle acceleration mechanisms, with future measurements key to confirming the model's predictions.

title: Testing X-ray selection effects with four rich, yet X--ray--faint, galaxy clusters
summary: A robust understanding of selection effects in galaxy cluster studies is crucial for both astrophysical and cosmological applications. Examining clusters identified through different observational strategies, even in small numbers, helps to illuminate potential biases inherent to each method. We selected four rich galaxy clusters in the Northern Hemisphere whose early Swift X-ray Telescope (XRT) observations indicated unusually low central X-ray emission, making them unlikely to be detected in X-ray surveys. Spectroscopic follow-up confirms that all four systems are genuine galaxy clusters, rather than projections of multiple clusters or groups along the line of sight. Their optical richness, estimated using one of the baseline Euclid cluster richness estimators, implies masses of $\log M_{200}/M_\odot \sim 14.6$ and independently confirms the absence of additional massive structures along the line of sight. Deep XRT follow-up reveals highly disturbed X-ray morphologies: three clusters exhibit at least two distinct X-ray peaks, while the remaining cluster has an axis ratio exceeding 1.5. Spectroscopy shows that galaxies associated with different parts share the same redshift, demonstrating that these substructures are physically connected rather than chance projections. These clusters display low central X-ray surface brightness and total X-ray luminosities suppressed by roughly one dex for their richness, making them undetectable in X-ray surveys as eROSITA. We estimate $\sim$20\% as a lower limit for the poorly sampled population, albeit based on a small sample. Our results demonstrate that even rich clusters in the northern $z<0.3$ Universe can be missed by X-ray selection and that the X-ray variety captured by X-ray surveys underestimates the true cluster diversity.

AI.tldr: This study identifies a population of rich galaxy clusters with low central X-ray brightness and disturbed morphologies that are missed by standard X-ray surveys, implying a significant selection bias and underestimation of cluster diversity in X-ray-based cluster catalogs.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify selection biases in galaxy cluster studies by examining clusters identified through different observational methods, focusing on clusters that appear underluminous in X-rays and may be missed in typical X-ray surveys.
AI.method: Selected four rich galaxy clusters from early Swift XRT observations that showed unusually low central X-ray emission; performed spectroscopic follow-up to confirm their nature and measure redshifts; estimated their masses using Euclid optical richness estimators; conducted deep XRT observations to analyze X-ray morphology and luminosity; compared these observations with typical X-ray survey detections.
AI.result: Confirmed that the four selected systems are genuine clusters with complex, disturbed X-ray morphologies and low central X-ray brightness, causing them to be underrepresented in X-ray surveys like eROSITA. They have significant mass but suppressed X-ray luminosities by about one dex relative to their optical richness. Estimated a minimum 20% fraction of such underluminous clusters that are likely missed in X-ray surveys.
AI.conclusion: Current X-ray surveys underestimate the diversity of galaxy clusters due to selection biases against clusters with disturbed morphologies and low central X-ray emission. This implies that even rich clusters at low redshift can be missed, affecting astrophysical and cosmological studies that rely on X-ray selected samples.

title: Accreting stellar-mass black holes
comment: 56 pages, 24 Figures. Submitted to SSRv. Comments welcome
summary: Accreting stellar-mass black holes exhibit dramatic variability across the electromagnetic spectrum, including spectral state transitions, outbursts, and jet production, making them unique laboratories for understanding accretion processes in strong gravitational fields. This review synthesizes recent progress in understanding these systems, focusing on their continuum emission, timing properties, emission lines, and X-ray polarization. A complex interplay between the accretion disk, the so-called corona, and jet underlies the observed spectral and timing behavior, with quasi-periodic oscillations and broadband noise providing windows into the dynamics of the innermost accretion flow. Emission lines across all wavelengths serve as critical diagnostics of disk structure, outflows, and reprocessing, while iron K lines in the X-ray band probe the properties of the inner disk through relativistic reflection. Polarization studies suggest that the corona is likely extended perpendicular to the jet axis in the hard state, while the soft state remains poorly understood, with observations that do not yet conform to simple theoretical expectations; a puzzle that continues to challenge our interpretation of accretion geometry. Despite significant advances, fundamental questions remain about the physical origins of state transitions, the role of magnetic fields in driving outflows and shaping the accretion flow, and the connection between disk instabilities and jet launching. This review underscores the need for future multi-wavelength, timing, and polarimetric studies to deepen our understanding of accretion physics in strong-gravity environments.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes recent advances in understanding the complex accretion processes around stellar-mass black holes through multi-wavelength observations and theoretical models, emphasizing the interplay between disk, corona, and jets, and outlining key open questions and future research directions.
AI.motivation: To understand accretion processes in strong gravitational fields by studying the variability of accreting stellar-mass black holes, which serve as unique laboratories due to their dramatic multi-wavelength variability including state transitions, outbursts, and jet production.
AI.method: A comprehensive review synthesizing recent observational and theoretical progress, focusing on continuum emission, timing properties (quasi-periodic oscillations and broadband noise), emission lines across the electromagnetic spectrum, and X-ray polarization studies.
AI.result: Key insights into the complex interactions between the accretion disk, corona, and jet are highlighted, including the role of emission lines and iron K lines as diagnostics, and polarization signatures suggesting corona geometry in different spectral states. Persistent challenges include understanding state transitions, magnetic field effects, and jet launching mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: While significant advancements have been made in characterizing the accretion flow and its variability in stellar-mass black holes, fundamental questions about the physical mechanisms governing state transitions, magnetic fields, and jet formation remain unresolved, necessitating future multi-wavelength, timing, and polarimetric observations.

title: The impact of evolving cosmic filaments on mass and spin evolution of dark matter halos
summary: The evolution of galaxies is closely tied to that of their host dark matter halos, which is in turn strongly modulated by the surrounding large-scale environment. Cosmic filaments are expected to influence the peculiar motions, mass assembly and angular momentum of nearby halos through highly anisotropic matter flows. In order to fully capture the dynamic interplay between the filaments and halos, we develop an algorithm to trace the progenitors of individual filaments identified at z=0 with DisPerSE in a cosmological N-body simulation, by quantifying the spatial similarity between a descendant filament and progenitor candidates. This enables us to reconstruct filament-by-filament evolutionary histories, including their bulk drift and the evolution of density profiles, from which splashback radii and core overdensities are derived. Using these time-dependent properties, we re-examine halo phase-space trajectories in a filament-centric frame that evolves with time. This eliminates biases inherent to static models by separating halo motions from the motion of the filaments, allowing trajectories to be identified more reliably. We find that as halos approach high-density filaments, their mass accretion rates are systematically suppressed beginning at the filament outskirts, suggestive of tidal stripping or suppressed net accretion. Furthermore, the evolution of halo spin alignments exhibits a clear departure from stochastic random-walk expectations. This suggests that distinct mass flow regimes in and around filaments exert different torques on infalling halos, thereby changing their angular momentum. Our findings, derived from a sample screened for major mergers, highlight the pure dynamical impact of the filamentary environment. Ultimately, we demonstrate that tracking the simultaneous co-evolution of filaments and halos is essential for accurately characterizing environmental effects.

AI.tldr: An algorithm tracing cosmic filaments in simulations reveals that nearby halos have suppressed mass accretion and altered spin growth due to filament environments, showing that modeling evolving filament-halo interactions is essential to understand galaxy evolution.
AI.motivation: To understand how cosmic filaments dynamically influence the evolution of dark matter halos and their interactions, considering the impact of large-scale environment on galaxy evolution.
AI.method: Developed an algorithm to trace progenitors of individual filaments over time in cosmological N-body simulations using DisPerSE, quantifying spatial similarity to reconstruct filament evolutionary histories and analyze halo trajectories in evolving filament-centric frames.
AI.result: Found that halos near high-density filaments experience suppressed mass accretion starting at filament outskirts, likely due to tidal stripping or reduced accretion; also observed non-random evolution of halo spin alignments influenced by filament mass flow regimes.
AI.conclusion: Tracking the co-evolution of filaments and halos with time-dependent filament-centric analysis is crucial to accurately capture environmental effects on halo dynamics, mass assembly, and angular momentum evolution.

title: Supernova Remnants in the IXPE era: a review
comment: To be published in the Multifrequency Behaviour of High Energy Cosmic Sources - XV Proceedings of Science 2025 issue: https://pos.sissa.it/506/
summary: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) has opened a new observational window on the physics of supernova remnants (SNRs) by providing the first spatially resolved X-ray polarimetry measurements. These data directly probe the geometry and turbulence of magnetic fields in regions of efficient particle acceleration, thereby constraining models of diffusive shock acceleration and magnetic-field amplification. IXPE has so far observed six young SNRs (Cas A, Tycho, SN 1006, RX J1713.7-3946, Vela Jr., and RCW 86) with published results on the first five. The observations reveal significant polarization in all cases, with degrees of polarization ranging from 5% to over 30%, reflecting different turbulence levels and environmental conditions. Three remnants (Cas A, Tycho, and SN 1006) show predominantly radial magnetic fields, while RX J1713.7-3946 and Vela Jr. display tangential morphologies. This dual behavior, not simply correlated with evolutionary stage, challenges the long-standing dichotomy inferred from radio observations and suggests that both shock velocity and circumstellar medium density play key roles in shaping magnetic-field topology. IXPE's results mark a major step toward disentangling the processes governing cosmic-ray acceleration in young SNR shocks, with ongoing and future observations expected to further constrain the interplay between turbulence, shock dynamics, and particle acceleration.

AI.tldr: IXPE's X-ray polarimetry of six young supernova remnants reveals diverse magnetic field structures that challenge previous radio-based models, improving understanding of the physics behind cosmic-ray acceleration in SNR shocks.
AI.motivation: To directly investigate the magnetic field geometry and turbulence in young SNRs to better understand mechanisms of diffusive shock acceleration and magnetic-field amplification in particle acceleration regions.
AI.method: Using X-ray polarimetry measurements from IXPE on six young supernova remnants, spatially resolved polarization data were analyzed to probe magnetic field structures and turbulence levels.
AI.result: All observed SNRs exhibit significant X-ray polarization indicating varying turbulence and environmental conditions; radial magnetic fields dominate in three remnants, while tangential fields are seen in two, showing that magnetic-field topology is influenced by more factors than previously thought.
AI.conclusion: IXPE's spatially resolved X-ray polarimetry observations provide critical insights into magnetic field geometries and turbulence in young SNRs, challenging previous assumptions and highlighting the roles of shock velocity and ambient density in magnetic-field topology and particle acceleration.

title: A self-consistent analytical model for both the photoionization rate and reionization history
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures (main text) + 4 pages (appendices). Prepared for submission to JCAP. Comments welcome!
summary: Recent developments at the intersection of cosmology and astrophysics have highlighted the need for improved analytical models of observables that probe the Epoch of Reionization. With few exceptions, fast analytical treatments of reionization suitable for use in Bayesian inference have been limited to modeling the reionization history, $x_i(z)$. Such models cannot take full advantage of observables that constrain $x_i$ indirectly. One such observable is the photoionization rate of neutral hydrogen, $Γ_{\rm HI}(z)$, which can be inferred from the mean transmission of the Lyman-$α$ forest of high-redshift quasars and galaxies. It has been shown by several prior works that the evolution of $Γ_{\rm HI}$ at $5 \lesssim z \lesssim 6$ is highly sensitive to the tail end of reionization, potentially providing a tight astrophysical constraint on the reionization timeline. We present a new analytical formalism, based on the cosmological radiative transfer equation, that self-consistently predicts $x_i$ and $Γ_{\rm HI}$. We test our model against detailed radiative transfer simulations and find it to be percent-level accurate in $x_i$ and $20-30\%$ accurate in $Γ_{\rm HI}$ at $z \lesssim 6$ - better than or comparable to existing observational uncertainties. Finally, we demonstrate that modest shifts in the ionizing photon output of high-redshift galaxies and/or the endpoint of reionization lead to differences in $Γ_{\rm HI}$ much larger that the model's intrinsic uncertainty, highlighting its utility for interpreting existing data. We explore the origin of modeling uncertainty in $Γ_{\rm HI}$ and comment on future pathways for improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a new analytical model using cosmological radiative transfer to predict the reionization history and photoionization rate, achieving high accuracy and demonstrating its value for constraining the Epoch of Reionization with current observations.
AI.motivation: Existing analytical models primarily focus on modeling the reionization history, $x_i(z)$, and cannot fully utilize observables that indirectly constrain $x_i$, such as the photoionization rate $Γ_{m HI}(z)$.
AI.method: The paper introduces a new analytical formalism based on the cosmological radiative transfer equation that predicts both the ionization fraction $x_i$ and the photoionization rate $Γ_{m HI}$ self-consistently.
AI.result: The model achieves percent-level accuracy in $x_i$ and 20-30% accuracy in $Γ_{m HI}$ for redshifts $z \lesssim 6$, comparable to or better than current observational uncertainties. It also shows that small variations in ionizing photon output or reionization endpoint significantly affect $Γ_{m HI}$ beyond model uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analytical model is a reliable tool for interpreting observables related to the Epoch of Reionization, particularly the photoionization rate, and it improves constraints on the reionization timeline. Future work should focus on reducing uncertainties in modeling $Γ_{m HI}$.

title: A Whisper from Within: Response of a Pulsar Timing Array to an Internal Gravitational-wave Source
summary: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are abundant in globular clusters (GCs) and probably also in galactic nuclei. They offer the potential to form a miniature pulsar timing array (mini-PTA) to detect nanohertz gravitational-wave (GW) sources located inside the array. Since the size of such an array is comparable to the wavelength of GW, the conventional plane-wave approximation becomes invalid, and near-field effects, including wavefront curvature, non-radiative self-field of the GW source, and direct perturbation of pulsar by GW, become significant. In this work, we incorporate these effects in a comprehensive model to calculate the timing residual induced by a GW source inside a mini-PTA. We also consider realistic GW source configurations in GCs (M15 and $ω$ Centauri) and in galactic nuclei (Sgr A* and M31), and find that for MSPs located sufficiently close to the GW source (within a few wavelengths), the residual can reach $1~μ\mathrm{s}$ in GCs and up to milliseconds in galactic centers, within the potential detection reach of current radio telescopes. Crucially, when the pulsar lies within a few GW wavelengths of the source, the non-radiative field dominates and causes the residual to rise much more steeply (between $1/r_e^2$ and $1/r_e^4$, where $r_e$ is the distance to the source) than the conventional far-field scaling ($1/r_e$). These results demonstrate that mini-PTAs in GCs or galactic nuclei can serve as powerful probes of otherwise invisible GW sources, including intermediate-mass and supermassive black hole binaries.

AI.tldr: This paper models near-field gravitational wave effects on millisecond pulsars in globular clusters and galactic nuclei, showing that small-scale pulsar timing arrays can detect nearby gravitational-wave sources with stronger signals than previously thought.
AI.motivation: To explore the potential of millisecond pulsars in globular clusters and galactic nuclei to form miniature pulsar timing arrays for detecting nanohertz gravitational-wave sources located nearby, overcoming limitations of the conventional plane-wave approximation.
AI.method: Developed a comprehensive model incorporating near-field effects such as wavefront curvature, non-radiative self-field of the GW source, and direct perturbation of pulsars by gravitational waves; applied this model to realistic GW source scenarios in specific globular clusters and galactic nuclei.
AI.result: Found that timing residuals induced by GW sources within a few wavelengths can reach microsecond levels in globular clusters and milliseconds in galactic centers, detectable by current radio telescopes; near-field non-radiative effects dominate and produce a steeper residual-distance scaling than far-field approximations.
AI.conclusion: Miniature pulsar timing arrays formed by millisecond pulsars in globular clusters and galactic nuclei can effectively probe gravitational-wave sources, such as intermediate-mass and supermassive black hole binaries, that are otherwise difficult to detect.

title: Validation of the Hybrid Bias Expansion model for the galaxy bispectrum
summary: The Hybrid Bias Expansion model (also known as Hybrid Effective Field Theory, HEFT) provides a promising way to extend the range of validity of perturbative large-scale structure modelling by replacing perturbative gravitational evolution with the nonlinear displacement field measured from $N$-body simulations. While this approach has already been shown to improve the modelling of the power spectrum, its validity at the bispectrum level has not yet been established. In this work we perform a first systematic real-space validation of the Hybrid bispectrum model using DESI-like LRG and ELG mock catalogues constructed at fixed cosmology on volumes similar to those of DESI's LRG samples. We find that the model remains self-consistent up to $k_{\rm max}^B \simeq 0.25\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, while clear signs of breakdown appear for a similar EFT tree-level bispectrum approach at $k_{\rm max}^B \gtrsim 0.13\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We also show that adding matter cross-statistics significantly improves the precision of the recovered bias parameters, while a partial third-order extension including only the $δ^3$ operator does not extend the validity range. Finally, we find a strong hierarchy among the bispectrum basis terms when grouped by total bias-operator order, with the lowest-order sectors dominating the total amplitude, which has important implications in emulation strategies.

AI.tldr: This work validates the Hybrid Bias Expansion model for the bispectrum, showing it reliably extends modeling accuracy to smaller scales than standard EFT methods and suggests efficient bias operator usage for large-scale structure analysis.
AI.motivation: Extend the validity of perturbative large-scale structure modeling by improving the bispectrum modeling with Hybrid Bias Expansion (HEFT) methods, which have shown promise for the power spectrum but lack bispectrum validation.
AI.method: Systematic real-space validation of the Hybrid bispectrum model using DESI-like LRG and ELG mock catalogs at fixed cosmology. Comparative analysis with EFT tree-level bispectrum approaches was performed, along with testing the impact of adding matter cross-statistics and partial third-order operator extensions.
AI.result: The Hybrid bispectrum model remains valid up to k_max^B ≈ 0.25 h/Mpc, outperforming EFT tree-level methods which break down beyond k_max^B ≈ 0.13 h/Mpc. Inclusion of matter cross-statistics enhances parameter precision, while partial third-order extensions do not extend validity. A hierarchy among bispectrum basis terms was observed, with lower-order sectors dominating the amplitude.
AI.conclusion: The Hybrid Bias Expansion model significantly improves bispectrum modeling range and precision compared to standard EFT approaches, although additional higher-order bias operators offer limited further gains. The observed bispectrum term hierarchy informs efficient emulation strategies for large-scale structure analysis.

title: A FAST search for radio pulsations during the dormant state of the AMSPs IGR J00291+5934 and MAXI J1957+032
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures; accepted for publication by A&A
summary: Accreting millisecond pulsars (AMSPs) and transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs) are neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries which can evolve into "recycled" radio millisecond pulsars. In both types of systems, X-ray pulsations have been detected during phases of X-ray activity when matter accretion through a disc is turned on. On the other hand, when accretion stops, and these systems enter the quiescent, low-luminosity X-ray state, only tMSPs become visible as radio pulsars. Despite several attempts, radio pulsations have never been detected in quiescent AMSPs, except for IGR J18245$-$2452. In this manuscript, we present the results of two observational campaigns performed on the AMSPs IGR J00291+5934 and MAXI J1957+032 with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope ($\it{FAST}$) in L-band (1-1.5 GHz). Both sources have most likely been observed in quiescence, as suggested by the upper limits on their X-ray and optical flux obtained with Swift and the Las Cumbres Observatory, respectively. We have performed a deep search for coherent periodicities in radio but found no significant candidate signal, either at the known spin frequency of those sources or at other frequencies. Assuming a pulse duty cycle of 10%, we derive upper limits on the pulsed radio flux density of 3.3 $μ$Jy and 5.6 $μ$Jy for IGR J00291+5934 and MAXI J1957+032, respectively, which are the most stringent limits so far for any known persistent AMSP.

AI.tldr: Deep radio observations with FAST of two quiescent accreting millisecond pulsars found no radio pulsations, placing the strongest upper limits yet on their radio emission and shedding light on the nature of pulsar emission states during low accretion phases.
AI.motivation: To investigate the presence of radio pulsations in accreting millisecond pulsars (AMSPs) during their quiescent states, which has not been conclusively detected except in rare cases, improving understanding of their emission states and evolutionary link to radio millisecond pulsars.
AI.method: Conducted two observational campaigns using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST) in L-band (1-1.5 GHz) targeting AMSPs IGR J00291+5934 and MAXI J1957+032 during quiescence. Utilized X-ray and optical flux upper limits from Swift and Las Cumbres Observatory to confirm quiescent state, followed by deep searches for coherent radio pulsations at known spin frequencies and other frequencies.
AI.result: No significant radio pulsations were detected from either source. Established upper limits on the pulsed radio flux densities of 3.3 μJy for IGR J00291+5934 and 5.6 μJy for MAXI J1957+032, representing the most stringent limits set so far for persistent AMSPs.
AI.conclusion: The absence of detectable coherent radio pulsations in quiescent AMSPs IGR J00291+5934 and MAXI J1957+032, despite deep searches with FAST, suggests that these sources either do not emit radio pulsations in quiescence or their emission lies below current sensitivity thresholds, providing key constraints on models of their transitional behavior and emission mechanisms.

title: Fireworks at Cosmic Dawn: relieving BAO-CMB tensions with the Pop III.1 Flash
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to ApJL, comments welcome
summary: A Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) optical depth of $τ\sim 0.09$, several $σ$ in excess of the latest Planck low-$\ell$ EE polarization measurement, has been proposed as a way to reconcile the preference for a sub-minimal neutrino mass sum in a combined analysis with CMB and Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) three-year data. Reionization, however, is not just probed by $τ$. It is also constrained by Ly$α$ forest observations that indicate a late end of reionization, and the patchy kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (pkSZ) effect which prefers a short duration. We explore whether an early phase of reionization can achieve a high $τ$ while remaining consistent with both Ly$α$ forest and pkSZ constraints. As a concrete example, we consider supermassive Pop III.1 stars, dark-matter-powered metal-free stars proposed as progenitors of supermassive black holes. Within this framework, self-regulating ionizing feedback imposes a minimum source separation of $\sim 1 \, \text{cMpc}$, consequently limiting large-scale ionization fluctuations and reducing the pkSZ power on observationally relevant scales. Our fiducial model realizes an optical depth of $τ= 0.087$ with a Pop III.1-driven flash ionization phase centered at $z = 20$, while evading the most conservative $2σ$ upper limits on the pkSZ signal from the most recent South Pole Telescope data release. More broadly, our findings motivate further exploration of early reionization models with weakly clustered sources as a possible resolution of tensions between BAO and CMB measurements.

AI.tldr: This study proposes early reionization by supermassive Pop III.1 stars to explain a high CMB optical depth while remaining consistent with Lyα forest and patchy kSZ constraints, indicating such models might resolve current cosmological parameter tensions.
AI.motivation: Reconciling the observed optical depth τ ∼ 0.09 — which is in tension with Planck low-ℓ EE polarization results — with combined CMB and DESI data that prefer sub-minimal neutrino mass sums, while satisfying additional constraints from Lyα forest and pkSZ observations that restrict the timing and duration of reionization.
AI.method: The authors model reionization including a self-regulating ionizing feedback mechanism leading to minimum source separation, which limits ionization fluctuations and pkSZ power. They test a scenario with Pop III.1 stars inducing a flash ionization phase at redshift z=20 and compare results against observational constraints such as τ from Planck, Lyα data, and pkSZ measurements from South Pole Telescope data.
AI.result: Their fiducial model achieves τ=0.087 with early reionization driven by Pop III.1 stars centered at z=20, remaining below conservative 2σ upper limits on pkSZ power and compatible with Lyα forest results, suggesting early reionization with weakly clustered sources can alleviate cosmological measurement tensions.
AI.conclusion: An early phase of reionization driven by supermassive Pop III.1 stars can produce a high optical depth (τ ≈ 0.087) consistent with both Lyα forest observations and pkSZ constraints, potentially resolving tensions between BAO and CMB measurements.

title: On the impact of the carbon fusion rate over the properties of superbursts -- Numerical simulations of superbursts with MESA
summary: Context: Superbursts are very energetic explosions in the crust of neutron stars in Low-Mass X-ray Binaries (LMXBs). These are triggered by unstable carbon burning at $T\leq 10^{9}$ K. In recent years, there has been a re-examination of the carbon fusion rate, finding that at these temperatures it might be either smaller or higher with respect to the classic rate from Caughler \& Fowler (1988) by a factor $10^{3}$. Aims: We explore the consequences changing the carbon fusion rate has over the physics of superbursts. Methods: For simulating superbursts, we employ the public code MESA v.24.08.1, as well as four versions of the carbon fusion reaction rate. Results: An enhancement of the reaction rate by a factor $10^{3}$ at $T\leq 10^9$~K reduces the recurrence and decay times of the superburst, as well as the column depth at ignition. The opposite behavior is observed when the carbon fusion rate is reduced by the same factor. The maximum temperature reached during the explosion is also sensitive to these changes, leading to either an enhancement or a reduction in the synthesis of $α$-nuclides. These changes are comparable to the effect of reducing the amount of base heating at the bottom of the envelope.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how variations in the carbon fusion rate by three orders of magnitude affect superburst properties in neutron star crusts. Enhanced rates lead to faster, shallower, and hotter bursts with increased nucleosynthesis, while reduced rates produce the opposite. These effects are comparable to changes in base heating, highlighting the critical role of carbon fusion rate uncertainties in superburst models.
AI.motivation: Recent updates suggest the carbon fusion rate at temperatures relevant for superbursts may differ significantly (by a factor of 10^3) from the classic rate, motivating an investigation into how these changes affect superburst physics.
AI.method: The study uses the MESA stellar evolution code (version 24.08.1) to simulate superbursts with four different versions of the carbon fusion reaction rate, systematically varying the rate by factors of 10^3.
AI.result: Increasing the carbon fusion rate by 10^3 at T ≤ 10^9 K leads to shorter superburst recurrence and decay times, shallower ignition column depths, higher peak temperatures, and enhanced synthesis of alpha-nuclides. Conversely, decreasing the rate results in the opposite effects. These variations mimic changes caused by altering base heating at the envelope's bottom.
AI.conclusion: Superburst characteristics—such as recurrence time, ignition depth, peak temperature, and nucleosynthesis—are highly sensitive to the carbon fusion rate, indicating that uncertainties in this rate significantly impact superburst modeling and interpretation.

title: Statistical Field Theory for Weak Gravitational Lensing
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures. Prepared for submission to PRD. A companion paper introducing the sft-wick formalism and package is submitted at the same time. Comments welcome
summary: Standard weak-lensing calculations treat lensing as a linear remapping of the matter field along the line of sight. We instead formulate lensing as a stochastic field theory for the Sachs optical scalars, driven by random Ricci-focusing and Weyl-shearing fields. The resulting path integral generates a diagrammatic expansion for arbitrary $n$-point correlation functions of lensing observables, organised into linear response, nonlinear propagation, and driving-field cumulants. The conventional calculation emerges as the lowest-order, linear-propagation limit. Beyond it, nonlinear Sachs evolution couples to driving-field non-Gaussianity, mixing the matter cumulant hierarchy into the lensing hierarchy. A selection rule governs the couplings: an $n$-point observable receives a direct contribution from the $n$-point driving-field cumulant, and its leading hierarchy-mixing correction from the $(n+1)$-point cumulant via one nonlinear Sachs interaction, with higher cumulants entering only at higher order. The two-point function, for instance, is corrected by squeezed three-point cumulants of Ricci focusing and Weyl shearing, letting small-scale modes source larger scales and feeding the lensing $E$- and $B$-modes equally. Rather than a restrictive approximation scheme, the formalism is a paradigm shift: a unified framework naturally accommodating path corrections, higher-order matter statistics, stochasticity, and small-scale effects.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a stochastic field theory approach to weak gravitational lensing, going beyond linear methods to include nonlinear and higher-order statistical effects of the matter field, offering a comprehensive framework for accurate lensing predictions.
AI.motivation: Standard weak-lensing calculations rely on a linear approximation that may miss important nonlinear effects and higher-order statistics in lensing observables.
AI.method: Formulating lensing as a stochastic field theory for Sachs optical scalars with random Ricci-focusing and Weyl-shearing fields, using a path integral approach and diagrammatic expansions for n-point correlation functions.
AI.result: The approach naturally reproduces conventional linear calculations as a limit, introduces nonlinear coupling between driving-field non-Gaussianity and Sachs evolution, and reveals a selection rule for hierarchy mixing in lensing cumulants, where higher-point cumulants influence lower-point observables at increasing orders.
AI.conclusion: This formalism constitutes a paradigm shift by providing a unified framework that incorporates nonlinear effects, higher-order matter statistics, stochasticity, and small-scale corrections in weak-lensing analysis beyond the traditional linear-remapping approximation.

title: Kick bimodality of neutron stars and mode dependence of their parameters
summary: Analysis of observational data and theoretical modeling favors a bimodal distribution of the natal velocity kick of neutron stars. For $\sim200$ normal isolated radio pulsars with well-determined spin and kinematic parameters, we determine if they belong to the low- or high-velocity mode of the distribution. Our results demonstrate that about $30\%$ belong to the low-velocity mode. We then analyze the differences in the properties of the two sets of pulsars. For some parameters (characteristic ages, distances, and radio luminosities), we see a clear difference between the two modes. However, for these quantities, it can be easily attributed to selection bias. For those parameters that are not a subject of strong selection, such as pulse width, we do not observe any difference. Interestingly, we detect a significant difference in the magnetic field distribution between the two modes. Lower field pulsars ($B\lesssim 10^{12}$~G) are overabundant among objects from the low-velocity mode in comparison to the high-velocity one. Among pulsars with low field ($\lesssim 10^{11}$~G), we do not identify any objects from the high-velocity mode of the kick distribution. The origin of this discrepancy is not clear, and we discuss several possibilities.

AI.tldr: This study confirms a bimodal natal kick velocity distribution in neutron stars, identifying distinct magnetic field distributions between low- and high-velocity pulsars, with low-field pulsars predominantly in the low-velocity group. The reasons behind the absence of low-field, high-velocity pulsars remain unclear.
AI.motivation: To understand the distribution of natal velocity kicks of neutron stars and how it correlates with pulsar properties.
AI.method: Analyzed observational data of ~200 isolated radio pulsars with well-determined spin and kinematic parameters to assign them to low- or high-velocity kick modes, followed by a comparative study of their physical and observational properties.
AI.result: Approximately 30% of pulsars belong to the low-velocity mode. Differences in characteristic ages, distances, and radio luminosities are likely affected by selection bias, while pulse width shows no difference. A significant difference in magnetic field distribution is observed: lower magnetic field pulsars are more common in the low-velocity mode, with no high-velocity objects below ~10^{11} G.
AI.conclusion: The bimodal velocity kick distribution is supported by the data, with a notable link between kick velocities and magnetic field strengths. The absence of low-field, high-velocity pulsars is unexplained and suggests new physics or selection effects that require further investigation.

title: Reheating as a variational probe of cosmological observables
summary: We formulate reheating as a constrained variational problem in the space of equation-of-state histories, rather than attempting to describe it through microscopic models. We introduce a regularized functional framework that identifies reheating histories which extremize a given cosmological observable under minimal physical assumptions. As illustrative applications, we consider prompt gravitational waves, induced gravitational waves, and primordial black holes. We find that different observables select qualitatively different regions of reheating-history space. These examples demonstrate that cosmological observables define distinct extremal directions in reheating-history space and can therefore be used to systematically explore the space of post-inflationary expansion histories.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel variational method to characterize reheating in cosmology by extremizing cosmological observables over possible equation-of-state histories, revealing that different observables pinpoint distinct reheating scenarios and enabling systematic exploration of post-inflationary expansion.
AI.motivation: To develop a model-independent framework for describing the reheating phase in cosmology without relying on detailed microscopic models.
AI.method: Formulating reheating as a constrained variational problem in the space of equation-of-state histories and introducing a regularized functional framework to identify reheating histories that extremize specific cosmological observables under minimal physical assumptions.
AI.result: Different cosmological observables select qualitatively different regions of reheating-history space, demonstrating that these observables define distinct extremal directions and allowing systematic exploration of post-inflationary expansion histories.
AI.conclusion: Cosmological observables can be used as tools to probe and constrain the space of reheating histories, providing a systematic approach to study post-inflationary dynamics without relying on detailed microscopic models.

title: Evidence for candidate X-ray pulsations from the ultraluminous X-ray source NGC 7456 ULX-1
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, to be published in ApJ
summary: We report evidence for a candidate pulsational signal at $\sim0.22$~Hz from NGC7456 ULX-1, a previously identified ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX). The signal is identified in the 2023 XMM-Newton observation using independent timing techniques including accelerated searches, $Z^2_n$ statistics, and an orbital-demodulation analysis designed to restore phase coherence in the presence of binary motion. The candidate pulsation frequency drift within the observation suggests rapid spin evolution driven by accretion torque. We further estimate the surface dipole magnetic field strength to be $B\sim 10^{12}-10^{14}$ G. These results provide evidence that NGC7456 ULX-1 may host an accreting neutron star, although confirmation with independent datasets or additional observations is required.

AI.tldr: Candidate pulsations detected at ~0.22 Hz in NGC7456 ULX-1 indicate an accreting neutron star with strong magnetic field, supported by timing analyses of 2023 XMM-Newton data; further confirmation is needed.
AI.motivation: To investigate the nature of NGC7456 ULX-1, an ultraluminous X-ray source, by searching for pulsational signals indicating the presence of an accreting neutron star.
AI.method: Using timing analysis techniques including accelerated searches, $Z^2_n$ statistics, and orbital-demodulation analysis on 2023 XMM-Newton observation data to detect pulsations and account for binary motion.
AI.result: Detected a candidate pulsational signal at ~0.22 Hz with frequency drift suggestive of rapid spin evolution due to accretion torque; estimated the neutron star's surface magnetic field strength to be ~$10^{12}-10^{14}$ G.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that NGC7456 ULX-1 may harbor an accreting neutron star, but further confirmation with independent data or additional observations is necessary.

title: Increasing the sensitivity of full-shape galaxy clustering measurements in configuration-space with three-point statistics
summary: We investigate the cosmological constraining power of a compressed line of sight dependent three point correlation function (3PCF) estimator on small scales (<80 Mpc/h) in configuration space, with a particular focus on emission line galaxies (ELGs) targeted by the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's Galaxy Redshift Survey (GRS), and complementary luminous red galaxy (LRG) samples observed by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). These scales avoid the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) feature and are therefore expected to provide information that is largely complementary to standard BAO measurements, while retaining partial overlap with full shape clustering analyses. Our forecasts are based on AbacusSummit simulations at z = 1.1 and z = 0.8, populated with galaxies using halo occupation distribution (HOD) models matched to Roman ELG and DESI LRG samples respectively. The three point measurements are computed with TriCo, a fast configuration space triangle counting code developed for this analysis. After marginalizing over uncertainties in the galaxy halo connection, we find that incorporating the 3PCF yields a substantial improvement over two point statistics alone, tightening the constraint on sigma_8 by a factor of 5 in our fiducial forecast. This gain arises not from a localized feature or specific scale range, but from the cumulative information content across triangle configurations. Restricting to the monopole of the 3PCF captures only part of this information, with the full line of sight dependent measurement providing an additional factor of 2 to 3 improvement over the monopole. Adding line of sight dependent three point information substantially increases the constraining power of small scale configuration space galaxy clustering.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the use of small scale, line of sight dependent three point correlation functions in galaxy surveys (Roman ELGs and DESI LRGs) to improve cosmological constraints, showing that incorporating full 3PCF information tightens sigma_8 constraints by a factor of 5 over two point statistics and provides complementary information to BAO and full shape analyses.
AI.motivation: To enhance cosmological parameter constraints by exploiting small scale three point correlation function (3PCF) measurements in galaxy surveys, particularly focusing on emission line galaxies targeted by Roman GRS and luminous red galaxies observed by DESI, beyond the information provided by BAO and two point statistics.
AI.method: Forecast cosmological constraints using line of sight dependent 3PCF estimators at scales less than 80 Mpc/h, based on AbacusSummit simulations populated with galaxies via halo occupation distribution models matching Roman ELG and DESI LRG samples. Computations of 3PCF were performed with TriCo, a fast triangle counting code in configuration space. The analysis involves marginalizing over uncertainties in galaxy-halo connection to quantify the additional constraining power of 3PCF relative to two point correlations.
AI.result: Incorporation of the full line of sight dependent 3PCF substantially tightens constraints on sigma_8, improving precision by a factor of 5 compared to two point statistics alone. The gain is due to cumulative information across triangle configurations rather than any single feature or scale. The monopole alone captures only part of this gain; including full line of sight dependence yields an additional factor of 2 to 3 improvement. Overall, the small scale 3PCF significantly enhances the cosmological constraining power of galaxy clustering measurements.
AI.conclusion: Line of sight dependent three point correlation function measurements on small scales provide substantial, complementary cosmological information beyond traditional two point statistics and BAO analyses, particularly for galaxy samples from Roman GRS and DESI. Utilizing the full 3PCF including its angular dependence greatly improves constraints on key cosmological parameters such as sigma_8, demonstrating the value of incorporating higher-order clustering statistics in future galaxy surveys.

title: Enhancing the Detection Sensitivity of Primordial Parity Violation using Galaxy Spins
summary: It has been recently demonstrated that the signature of primordial parity violation could be imprinted in halo spins, indicating its potential detectability through the late-time galaxy spin field (Shim et al. 2025). In this study, we develop an optimized halo selection strategy to enhance the detection significance of such a signal, focusing on halo mass and local density. Using N-body simulations with parity-asymmetric initial conditions, we show that the optimized halo sample allows for a higher detection sensitivity than the full halo sample, despite its reduced sample size. Finally, we assess the observational feasibility of our strategy and show that future spectroscopic surveys can provide sufficient data to realize this enhanced sensitivity.

AI.tldr: This study presents an optimized halo selection method to enhance detection of primordial parity violation in galaxy spins, demonstrating improved sensitivity with simulations and showing feasibility for future surveys.
AI.motivation: To detect the signature of primordial parity violation imprinted in halo spins through late-time galaxy spin fields.
AI.method: Developed an optimized halo selection strategy focusing on halo mass and local density, and used N-body simulations with parity-asymmetric initial conditions to test detection sensitivity.
AI.result: Optimized halo samples yield higher detection sensitivity for primordial parity violation signals compared to full halo samples, despite smaller sample sizes; future spectroscopic surveys can feasibly collect sufficient data to implement this strategy.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing halo selection based on mass and local density significantly improves the detectability of primordial parity violation signals in galaxy spin fields, making future observational efforts promising.

title: The stability of voids in the local Universe: the role of the cosmological constant
